plain_english:
Aren't you ashamed of being more cowardly and pathetic than runaway slaves? When slaves escape, what do they leave behind? What property do they count on? What servants do they have helping them? They steal a little food for the first few days, then figure out how to survive as they go — traveling by land or sea, coming up with one plan after another to stay alive. Has a runaway slave ever starved to death? But you're terrified that you won't have what you need, and you lie awake at night worrying. You fool, are you so blind that you can't see where lacking necessities actually leads? Well, where does it lead? To the same place that fever leads, or a falling stone — to death. Haven't you said this to your friends many times? Haven't you read plenty about this and written about it too? How often have you bragged that you were comfortable with death?

So first learn what things are actually shameful. Then tell us you're a philosopher. But right now, don't call yourself one — even if someone else does.
original_excerpt:
Are you not ashamed at being more cowardly and more mean than fugitive slaves? How do they when they run away leave their masters? on what estates do they depend, and what domestics do they rely on? Do they not after stealing a little, which is enough for the first days, then afterwards move on through land or through sea, contriving one method after another for maintaining their lives? And what fugitive slave ever died of hunger? But you are afraid lest necessary things should fail you, and are sleepless by night. Wretch, are you so blind, and don't you see the road to which the want of necessaries leads?—Well, where does it lead?—to the same place to which a fever leads, or a stone that falls on you, to death. Have you not often said this yourself to your companions? have you not read much of this kind, and written much? and how often have you boasted that you were easy as to death?

Learn then first what are the things which are shameful, and then tell us that you are a philosopher: but at present do not, even if any other man calls you so, allow it.
source_reference: Discourses, To Those Who Fear Want, Section 1

plain_english: Are you really ashamed of something that isn't your fault? Something you didn't cause? Something that just happened to you, like a headache or fever? If your parents were poor and left their money to someone else, if they don't help you while they're alive — are you ashamed of that? Is this what you learned from philosophers? Didn't you ever hear that only blameworthy things should make you ashamed? And that you can only blame people for their own actions? Who do you blame for something they didn't do themselves? Did you make your father who he is? Can you change him? Do you have that power? No. So should you want things you can't have? Should you be ashamed when you don't get them? Have you been studying philosophy just to depend on other people and expect nothing from yourself?
original_excerpt: Is that shameful to you which is not your own act, that of which you are not the cause, that which has come to you by accident, as a headache, as a fever? If your parents were poor, and left their property to others, and if while they live, they do not help you at all, is this shameful to you? Is this what you learned with the philosophers? Did you never hear that the thing which is shameful ought to be blamed, and that which is blamable is worthy of blame? Whom do you blame for an act which is not his own, which he did not do himself? Did you then make your father such as he is, or is it in your power to improve him? Is this power given to you? Well then, ought you to wish the things which are not given to you, or to be ashamed if you do not obtain them? And have you also been accustomed while you were studying philosophy to look to others and to hope for nothing from yourself?
source_reference: Discourses, To Those Who Fear Want, Section 1

plain_english: Go ahead then. Cry and moan and eat in fear that you might not have food tomorrow. Shake with worry about your poor slaves — that they might steal from you, run away, or die. Keep living like this. Keep it up, you who have only touched philosophy in name and have disgraced its teachings as much as you can. You've shown them to be worthless and useless to anyone who tries them. You've never looked for steadiness, peace of mind, or freedom from your emotions. You've never sought out any teacher for these goals — only many teachers for clever arguments. You've never seriously examined any of these situations by asking yourself: Can I handle this, or can't I? What should I do next? Instead, as if everything in your life were fine and safe, you've been focused on the third topic — keeping things unchanged. But what are you trying to keep unchanged? Your cowardice, your small spirit, your worship of rich people, your desires that never get satisfied, and your avoidance that always fails. This is what you've been worried about protecting.
original_excerpt: Lament then and groan and eat with fear that you may not have food to-morrow. Tremble about your poor slaves lest they steal, lest they run away, lest they die. So live, and continue to live, you who in name only have approached philosophy, and have disgraced its theorems as far as you can by showing them to be useless and unprofitable to those who take them up; you, who have never sought constancy, freedom from perturbation, and from passions; you who have not sought any person for the sake of this object, but many for the sake of syllogisms; you who have never thoroughly examined any of these appearances by yourself, Am I able to bear, or am I not able to bear? What remains for me to do? But as if all your affairs were well and secure, you have been resting on the third topic, that of things being unchanged, in order that you may possess unchanged—what? cowardice, mean spirit, the admiration of the rich, desire without attaining any end, and avoidance ([Greek: echchlisin]) which fails in the attempt? About security in these things you have been anxious.
source_reference: Discourses, To Those Who Fear Want, Section 1

plain_english: Shouldn't reason have given you something more? Shouldn't you protect that something? Have you ever seen someone build a wall around nothing? What good is a guard with no door to watch? But you practice just to prove things — prove what exactly? You practice so arguments won't confuse you — but confuse you about what? First show me what you actually believe. What are you measuring? Show me your scales. How long will you keep measuring dust? You should be proving the things that make people happy. The things that help life go the way they want. Why we shouldn't blame anyone or accuse anyone. Why we should accept how the universe works.
original_excerpt: Ought you not to have gained something in addition from reason, and then to have protected this with security? And whom did you ever see building a battlement all around and encircling it with a wall? And what doorkeeper is placed with no door to watch? But you practise in order to be able to prove—what? You practise that you may not be tossed as on the sea through sophisms, and tossed about from what? Show me first what you hold, what you measure, or what you weigh; and show me the scales or the medimnus (the measure); or how long will you go on measuring the dust? Ought you not to demonstrate those things which make men happy, which make things go on for them in the way as they wish, and why we ought to blame no man, accuse no man, and acquiesce in the administration of the universe?
source_reference: Discourses, To Those Who Fear Want, Section 1
